concept.name: Sterling ratio
concept.definition: A risk-adjusted return measure that divides the compound annual return by a function of average annual drawdown — originally, per Deane Sterling Jones (1981), the compound rate of return divided by the absolute value of (average annual drawdown minus 10%); modern variants use excess return over the average largest drawdown.
concept.intuition: Where Calmar charges only for the single worst drawdown, the Sterling ratio charges for the typical yearly drawdown: the routine pain, not just the record pain.
concept.mechanics: Compute each calendar year's worst peak-to-trough loss, average those drawdowns, and divide the compound annual return by that average adjusted by 10% (the original 1981 T-bill reference); the Sharpe-like modern form subtracts the risk-free rate in the numerator instead. Multiple definitions coexist in practice.
concept.formula: Original: SR = CompoundROR / |AvgAnnualDD - 10%|; modern variant: SR = (Annual portfolio return - annual risk-free rate) / average largest drawdown.
concept.failure_modes: The definition is not standardized — the 10% adjustment, the averaging convention, and the drawdown definition vary — so quoted Sterling ratios are frequently non-comparable across sources. Averaging drawdowns also dilutes the impact of one catastrophic year.
concept.misconceptions: The 10% in the original denominator is not a universal constant — it was the 1981 T-bill yield used as the risk-free benchmark — and the Sterling ratio is not just Calmar under another name: they use different drawdown aggregates.
concept.example: A fund compounding 18% annually with a 12% average annual maximum drawdown has an original-form Sterling ratio of 18 / |12 - 10| = 9, versus 1.5 on the modern excess-return form — illustrating the convention problem.
